hallucinations.claim: "There's no pharmacokinetic interaction ... the two drugs are metabolized by different CYP pathways"
hallucinations.why: Magnesium is a mineral and is not CYP-metabolised; the conclusion (no interaction) is right but the stated mechanism is invented.

hallucinations.claim: "Glycinate ... it's the safest choice for people already on an SSRI"
hallucinations.why: No evidence the magnesium form matters for SSRI safety; the reference says neither form interacts with sertraline and the choice is gut tolerance and price.

hallucinations.claim: "Heavy drinking (more than 3 drinks) can increase renal magnesium loss"
hallucinations.why: The '>3 drinks' threshold is invented, and the same paragraph admits 'no specific standard drink threshold was found in the evidence'.

hallucinations.claim: "high-dose citrate (above ~300 mg elemental) may worsen that GI irritation"
hallucinations.why: A specific cutoff with no source in the packet; it is near the NIH 350 mg supplemental UL but is presented as a citrate-specific threshold.

hallucinations.claim: "Some liquid or powdered glycinate products contain added sugar or aspartame"
hallucinations.why: Added by the reviewer with no source; an irrelevant tangent stated as a known concern.

what_went_wrong: The single gpt-oss:20b writer never squarely answered 'glycinate vs citrate: marketing?' and the ministral reviewer's notes pulled in a sugar/aspartame tangent and a meta sentence ('no threshold was found in the evidence') that leaked into the final text; it also skipped 'tell your prescriber'.
great_answer_would: Give three one-line answers: no known sertraline interaction (mention it to the prescriber), a few drinks are fine but heavy drinking depletes magnesium, and glycinate vs citrate is mostly marketing, choose by gut tolerance and price.
notes: Core sertraline verdict (no interaction) is correct and no trap (serotonin syndrome, hard spacing rule) was asserted. The opening line 'Take glycinate or citrate if you're on sertraline' reads as advice to take it because of sertraline. Turn 1 was an error, so the asker never got the dose/evidence answer either.

hallucinations.claim: "The Mayo Clinic article (May 2025) stresses that sudden, persistent odor shifts can signal a health problem"
hallucinations.why: The article is among the search results but the 'May 2025' date cannot be verified from the packet and looks invented.

hallucinations.claim: "Cut back on foods high in sulfur and keep hydrated to dilute sweat"
hallucinations.why: 'Hydration dilutes sweat odour' has no source; the odour comes from bacteria acting on apocrine sweat, not concentration.

hallucinations.claim: "Use a regular soap or an antibacterial soap; antibacterial soaps with certain claims are banned in the U.S. since 2016."
hallucinations.why: Garbled: the 2016 FDA rule removed triclosan and 18 other actives from consumer antiseptic washes (effective 2017); it did not ban 'antibacterial soaps with certain claims'. The line also recommends and warns against the same product.

what_went_wrong: Search returned content-farm pages plus Mayo, and the gpt-oss draft gave a generic hygiene list. It never named the fixes that actually work (10-20% aluminium chloride at night, benzoyl peroxide or chlorhexidine wash, hot or enzyme laundry for polyester) or the odour-type red flags, and it closed with the recap Pat asked not to get.
great_answer_would: Give one line on the bacteria mechanism, the likely causes of a change (stress, SSRIs or other meds, diet or keto, polyester), the fix stack in order (night-time aluminium chloride, a BPO wash for 2 weeks, cotton plus hot or enzyme wash), then the red-flag smells.
notes: Mechanism and 'antiperspirant before bed' are right. Calling fabrics a 'secondary factor' undersells polyester odour retention. No specific products, strengths or steps despite Pat's preference for exact numbers.

hallucinations.claim: "Hawaiian pizza ... brings ≈7 g fat per 3 oz (≈25 g) of ham"
hallucinations.why: 3 oz is about 85 g, not 25 g; the unit conversion is wrong and the per-serving figure is untraceable (source was a Mashed listicle).

hallucinations.claim: "less than the 8-10 g fat you'd get from a comparable amount of pepperoni or sausage"
hallucinations.why: 3 oz of pepperoni carries roughly 35+ g fat; the figure is invented and badly understates the gap.

hallucinations.claim: "(USDA FoodData Central, 2023)" for 250 kcal, 12 g fat, 4 g sat, 30 g carbs, 2-3 g fiber, 600-800 mg sodium
hallucinations.why: USDA FDC was not among the search sources; the '2023' citation is invented. The figures are in a plausible range (FDC regular-crust cheese slice is about 285 kcal, 10 g fat, 640 mg sodium) but are attributed to a source the run never saw.

hallucinations.claim: "deep-dish Chicago style slice can reach 400-500 kcal and 800-1,200 mg sodium"
hallucinations.why: Unsourced specific range; the Eater source is about whether deep dish is pizza, not nutrition.

hallucinations.claim: "People often crave pizza because it releases serotonin"
hallucinations.why: Pop-science claim taken from the Thought Catalog page at the reviewer's request; no evidence that pizza 'releases serotonin'.

hallucinations.claim: "Frozen pizza brands like DiGiorno tend to have higher calories and sodium"
hallucinations.why: Asserted, then disowned in the same sentence ('the specific values for DiGiorno are not supported'); unverified.

what_went_wrong: Search returned junk (a 2013 Thought Catalog photo guide, Mashed, an Eater debate), and the ministral reviewer told the writer to add serotonin cravings and extreme-crust comparisons. The merge leaked a verifier note mid-sentence ('...are not supported. but they often...') and a '****' formatting bug.
great_answer_would: Say no, 1-2 times a week is fine, in the first line. Give the typical NY slice numbers (~250-350 kcal, 600-800 mg sodium; 2-3 slices is a 1,500-2,000 mg sodium meal), name processed meat, extra cheese and portion as the problems with the fixes, and stay under 150 words.
notes: Sodium 2,300 mg and saturated fat at or under 10% of calories are correct. '2-3 times a week' is looser than the sheet's 1-2 but not absurd. It mixes slices and servings when giving frequency. The answer is about 2x the length the question needs and ends with a recap.

hallucinations.claim: "The 'Chronotype' article outlines a clinically tested protocol that moves extreme night-owl schedules two hours earlier"
hallucinations.why: The cited source is a retailer blog (kashmiril.com); it cannot stand as a clinical test. The real evidence, Facer-Childs et al. 2019 (Birmingham, Sleep Medicine), is not named.

hallucinations.claim: "the shift usually takes weeks to months"
hallucinations.why: The Birmingham protocol produced about a 2-hour advance in 3 weeks; 'months' has no source.

hallucinations.claim: "night owls sometimes show structural brain differences that could lead to health problems"
hallucinations.why: Vague overclaim from a blog; the Birmingham imaging work found resting-state connectivity differences, not structural ones linked to health problems.

hallucinations.claim: "early rising can boost mood for many" (backed by a LifeHack quote)
hallucinations.why: A LifeHack quote is used as the evidence; the actual literature is correlational, modest, and largely explained by social jetlag.

what_went_wrong: Search returned LifeHack, a shop blog, BBC and A.Vogel but no primary research. The gpt-oss writer quoted the blogs as evidence and missed the key explanation (social jetlag and sleep loss), and the review loop skipped verify.
great_answer_would: Call it half true: owls report modestly worse mood, mostly from schedule mismatch. Cite the 2019 Birmingham study (~2 h shift in 3 weeks), then give the five-step protocol (fixed wake time including weekends, morning bright light, dim evenings, earlier meals and caffeine cutoff, optional 0.5 mg melatonin) and warn that forcing the schedule without the light cues just makes a sleep-deprived owl.
notes: The '~2 hours earlier' figure is right, though sourced to a blog. No protocol steps were given despite Pat's preference for exact steps, and the closing paragraph is a recap.

hallucinations.claim: "many public figures—such as Joe Rogan, David Beckham, and the cast of The Mandalorian—have embraced the shaved or buzzed look"
hallucinations.why: Beckham is not balding and is known for varied full hairstyles; 'the cast of The Mandalorian' is nonsense. Only Rogan fits. The reviewer asked for celebrity references and the writer invented them.

hallucinations.claim: "A longer buzz (5-10 mm) ... requires more frequent trimming and can highlight scalp bumps or scars"
hallucinations.why: Backwards: a longer buzz shows regrowth less (so needs less frequent trimming) and hides scalp bumps and scars better than a short buzz or a shave.

hallucinations.claim: Table: full shave "~14 min" per week, "$1-$3" monthly in blades, "Shave 1-3 days a week"
hallucinations.why: Invented precise figures. 'Shave 1-3 days a week' contradicts the text's 'every 1-3 days', and cartridge blades usually cost more than $1-3 a month.

hallucinations.claim: "Daily SPF 30+ is often recommended by dermatologists for shaved scalp protection"
hallucinations.why: Broadly true (the AAD recommends SPF 30+ on exposed skin); not a hallucination, but hedged into mush ('adjust based on your skin type').

what_went_wrong: The gpt-oss draft had the right pick (buzz it all short), but the ministral reviewer pushed in celebrity references, so the merge added invented examples, a contradictory table and hedged face-shape filler. It never said plainly that keeping the long sides (the horseshoe) is the look to avoid, and it skipped the beard.
great_answer_would: Pick a #1-#2 buzz all over (or a shave if he will keep it up), say plainly that keeping the sides longer than a bald top is the one look to lose, give maintenance in a line each, and add a beard and daily scalp sunscreen, in under 150 words.
notes: The core pick (buzz top 1-2 mm, sides 1-3 mm, i.e. short all over) matches the sheet. The 'keep the sides?' part of the question went unanswered. Face-shape bullets are content-free hedges. It ends with an 'In short' recap.

hallucinations.why: A TikTok discover page is presented as 'science-based'; the timeline cannot be checked against that source. The real withdrawal timeline (peak days 3-7, fading over 2-4 weeks, cravings 3-5 minutes) is missing.

hallucinations.claim: "Check the NYC Department of Health website for a local toll-free quit line"
hallucinations.why: Vague pointer that sends him to hunt; the actual lines (1-800-QUIT-NOW, NYS Smokers' Quitline 1-866-NY-QUITS) are not named. More an omission than an invention.

what_went_wrong: Search returned TikTok, a vape-shop blog, wikiHow and a rehab-center ad instead of smokefree.gov or CDC, so the gpt-oss writer cited TikTok as science and never mentioned NRT, varenicline or the quitline. The review-only loop (no verify) let in contradictions: 'check-ins a few times a week' versus 'once a week'.
great_answer_would: Give one short script ('don't ask daily; snappy for two weeks is withdrawal; distract me; no lecture if I slip; Sunday check-in, my call'), the withdrawal timeline in one line, and the aids (patch plus gum or lozenge, varenicline, 1-800-QUIT-NOW), with 'the patch is the plan, not cheating', in under 200 words.
notes: The support-not-surveillance framing, the scripts, the slip-without-shame advice and a self-chosen cadence match the sheet well. Some lines are odd ('if I'm in the kitchen or watching TV, don't ask about vaping'; 'call you for a quick chat' has confused pronouns). It runs well over 200 words and closes with a recap.
